subject: axolotl
pitch: A tiny pink axolotl grinning up at you, three feathery gill fronds on each side of its head puffed out like a lion's mane, stubby four-toed hands, a ribbon tail. Chibi proportions: head as big as the body, glossy eyes, candy colours.
reasoning:
I need to plan out a full module efficiently, aiming for roughly 500-800 lines since correctness matters without being able to test it. I'm thinking through the design of a tiny chibi axolotl, with a real axolotl being about 0.2m long, so I'll scale proportions with an oversized head typical of chibi style.

I'll make it about 0.25-0.28m long, with a wide grinning head tilted up, separate upper/lower jaw for the smile, and feathery gill fronds puffed out like a mane built from tapered sweeps with filament cards. For the skeleton I'm planning a hips root joint, a spine chain running to a neck and head, a tail chain of several joints, and leg chains branching off.

Now I'm laying out coordinates: head centered forward and up with pitch tilted upward for the grin, body sized to roughly match the head's volume for a chibi look, and a tall flattened ribbon tail extending backward with an S-curve and a dorsal fin membrane in pink with lighter edges.

I'm sketching the skeleton next — hips as root, a short spine chain running forward, a head joint tilted upward off the spine tip, and a jaw joint positioned beneath the mouth.

For positioning, I'll rely on the `head.local` helper with directional words (forward, up, left, etc.) so placements stay consistent regardless of orientation, and I'm planning to build the head itself from a scaled sphere part attached to the head bone.

I'm weighing whether the sphere needs its own orientation to match the head's tilt, but deciding it's simpler to keep the skull geometry world-axis-aligned and just give the head joint a slight tilt direction, since decal placement via surface mapping should still work fine on top of it.

Working out rotation math...

Given the uncertainty around the region API, I'll skip relying on it and instead write my own helper function to map head-local coordinates to model space with the pitch applied directly.

Now I'm designing the skull surface as a low-poly ellipsoid for sampling nearest-point placement, and planning the head's coloring as a leucistic axolotl pink with countershading between back and belly, plus blush cheek decals.

For the mouth, I'm structuring the head as a wide, blunt chibi skull ellipsoid with a separate flattened lower jaw ellipsoid, and draping a dark pink smile curve along the surface to form the grin line.

Actually, I'll pose the jaw open about 10° around the hinge axis, then add a dark rose ellipsoid for the mouth interior plus a pink tongue shape, positioning the jaw bone and hinge coordinates so the opening reveals the mouth naturally against the upper skull.

Switching to a decal approach instead: a wide D-shaped smile with dark interior, tongue, and corner dimples projected across the skull and jaw surfaces, keeping the jaw itself closed and separate. The jaw ellipsoid pokes out slightly below the head front to form the chin.

For the eyes, I want to go bigger and glossier than real axolotl eyes to fit the chibi look -- dark navy ellipsoid spheres with layered white highlight spheres for a glossy anime-style shine, or alternatively a custom SVG decal with an iris and highlights drawn to match the same cute aesthetic.

Still defining eyeball decal and placement...

For eyeball placement, I'm using nearest-point lookup to seat the sphere into the skin surface with partial embedding so it sinks halfway in, then treating that hit as a decal target where the normal direction determines outward facing — though I need to make sure the eye orientation actually points forward rather than just following the surface normal.

Since the drawing is symmetric except for highlight placement, I'll just put both highlights upper-left for consistent lighting rather than mirroring. For the decal sizing, a 0.02 radius sphere with a 0.036 patch decal should fully cover the visible eyeball front, so I can draw the eye as a simple opaque circle within its viewBox.

For the eye texture itself, I'm designing a deep plum iris with a magenta glow underneath, a near-black pupil, and layered highlights (one large, one small, plus a tiny sparkle), with dark plum covering the rest of the eyeball sphere. I'm also planning tiny nostril dots on the snout and blush decals using rose-pink ellipses positioned lower on the cheeks, angled slightly outward and downward on the skull.

Since the texture uses alpha-cutoff rather than blending, I need the blush shapes to be solid above the cutoff threshold—so I'll draw them as solid darker pink ellipses with lighter hatch lines rather than relying on transparency. Now I'm working out the gill fronds, a key feature meant to puff out like a lion's mane: three fronds per side positioned behind the head, fanning in different directions—top frond angled up and back, middle frond outward, lower frond angled down—to create that puffed, mane-like silhouette.

Each frond needs a curved tapered stalk plus a ring of fine filaments along it, similar to a real axolotl gill plume. I'm considering building these as thin tapered geometric spikes extending outward from points along each stalk, with a color gradient running from dark red at the root to hot pink at the tip, while keeping the total part count manageable within budget.

Defining gill geometry function...

Working out filament placement...

Filament length tapers toward the tip, with roughly 12 per frond split between both sides, 72 total, radii shrinking from base to tip. I'm settling on a color gradient from deeper raspberry/coral at the roots to lighter pink at the tips so the gills read clearly against the body.

For texture needs, I'll keep it modest—eye, grin, blush, and maybe a sparkle detail should cover the requirement without overcomplicating things. For the body itself, I'm sweeping an ellipse profile along the spine chain, adjusting the belly offset so it sits properly on the floor.

Still shaping the body-tail tube...

Writing fin membrane geometry...

I'll extend the fin along the whole body as one continuous tube rather than just the tail, tapering its height from the chest down to nothing and growing toward the tail root. I'm also realizing the body is mostly hidden behind the oversized head — only a short visible stretch between the head's back and the hips, since the head takes up so much of the length.
